course_description:
This course will examine contemporary issues arising in the legal profession. Topics will vary from year to year, drawing on the innovative research of TC Beirne School of Law academic staff, as well as the expertise of visiting scholars and leading practitioners. Please refer to the Law School website for current topics.

This course will examine contemporary professional issues in the law of evidence, civil liability, civil litigation, ethics, and administrative tribunals.

Semester 2, 2026 Topic: Doing Business Internationally (China* and Australia) .

*For the purposes of this course, unless otherwise stated, China means Mainland China, not including Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan.

This course provides a high-level overview of the key matters to consider when doing business in and between Australia and China.

This course adopts a comparative law perspective and considers key business law topics, including the relevant legal and regulatory systems, establishing a legal presence in each jurisdiction, corporate governance, mergers and acquisitions of private companies, contract formation and enforcement, lending and taking security, restructuring and insolvency issues, and resolving commercial disputes.

The course will be conducted as 8 seminars of 3 hours each. The seminars will address the following topics:

COURSE AIMS

This is an interactive course taught in seminar mode.ﾠWe will be using an interactive method of teaching at times, so you may be called upon to contribute during the seminars. You are encouraged to turn your phones off during the seminars, and to limit use of your laptops when we are engaging in discussion. The course will be taught by Dr Carl Hinze.

course_aims:
Education Mission Statement

The mission of the School of Law is to educate you in and about the law. We seek to assist you to think critically about the law and to investigate its structures, principles, policies, and values. This is achieved by engaging with you as fellow investigators in a range of critical and intellectual conversations about the law and its place in society. Our role is thus to guide you in your own intellectual journey in the law and to equip you with the necessary skills that will enable you to continue that journey long after you have left the School.

Course Aims

learning_outcomes.description: Analyse the foundational principles, sources, and institutional structures of diverse legal traditions across Australia and China (e.g., common law vs. civil law).
Evaluate how historical, socio-political, economic, and cultural factors shape different legal systems and substantive norms in Australia and China.
Identify the relative strengths, weaknesses, and functional equivalents of legal concepts across the Australian and Chinese jurisdictions.

Independently locate, interpret, and evaluate primary and secondary legal sources (e.g., constitutions, statutes, and jurisprudence) from Australia and China on fundamental commercial law matters affecting business in Australia and China.
Articulate complex comparative legal analyses and theories to both specialist (legal practitioners) and non-specialist (client) audiences, both orally and in writing.

assessment_details.title: Group Presentation
assessment_details.task_description: By the end of the seminar in Week 2, students will form a small group (3-5 students). You will be given opportunities for group formation during the seminars in Weeks 1 and 2, and you may choose your own group members. Your assessment task will be a group presentation. Your group will choose one of the 8 seminar topics addressed during this course. During the group presentation, you will discuss the chosen topic, explain your research and present your ideas as to how the laws and regulations of Australia and China compare in regard to the chosen topic. The assessment is designed to test the following skills and competencies: Legal research — the ability to identify and engage with primary legal sources (legislation, regulations, administrative guidance) in both jurisdictions. Comparative legal analysis — the ability to identify meaningful similarities and differences between the two legal systems as they apply to the chosen topic. Issue identification and prioritisation — the ability to identify the most material legal issues from a practical perspective and to exercise sound judgement in prioritising those issues. Oral presentation — the ability to communicate complex legal matters clearly, concisely, and in an oral presentation format appropriate to the context. Application — the ability to apply general legal principles to the specific topic within a group context. Due date The group presentation will take place in Week 5. In class, you will be shown how to book a timeslot for your group presentation. Format All group members must be present for the presentation. Your group will be presenting to the course coordinator and fellow students. You may use a single page handout to support your in-person presentation. Powerpoint presentations are not allowed. Group input All group members must contribute to selecting, developing, researching, and presenting the topic. The oral component of the presentation will be shared among group members, and all group members must be prepared to answer questions during the Q&A component. Every group member will receive the same mark, unless a case is made otherwise. Two assessors will review the presentation to provide moderation of grades. learning_activities.topic: Legal and regulatory system This session will give a high-level overview of the key legal and regulatory systems in each of China and Australia, including the role of the constitution, system of governance and the general legislative process; the main sources of law; the court structure and hierarchy; the judiciary and its appointment and the general rules of civil and criminal litigation. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Formation of business entities When entering the market in Australia or China, whether by establishing a new subsidiary, joint venture, or through acquisition of an existing business, it is important to understand the differences among the trading vehicles available in each jurisdiction. Many trading vehicle types appear similar across jurisdictions and seem distinguished by name only. However, several key differences exist in the details. Understanding the differences helps an investor choose a trading vehicle that best suits their business purposes in the relevant jurisdiction. Australia and China offer several alternative methods for establishing a business and engaging in local commercial activities. The choice of trading vehicles will vary depending on the development of local laws as influenced by local economic and political systems, and cultural norms. This session provides an overview of the key corporate features of different trading vehicles that are commonly used when setting up a business in Australia and China. This session also provides an overview of the government approvals and business registration processes required for investors establishing a business in Australia and China. Finally, this session discusses the factors to be considered when choosing a structure and sets out the advantages and disadvantages of the most investment structures in Australia and China. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Corporate governance This session provides an overview of the corporate governance regime for companies operating in each of Australia and China. This session examines the core governance framework in each jurisdiction, detailing the respective rights and duties of shareholders as well as the specific powers and liabilities assigned to directors and senior management. It addresses key operational procedures affecting governance, including the quorum and voting rules for shareholders' meetings and board of directors' meetings, and instances where there may be a piercing of the 'corporate veil'. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Mergers & acquisitions (private) This session examines the typical stages of a corporate transaction involving private companies in each of Australia and China, from pre-contractual negotiations to post-closing procedures. It highlights critical jurisdiction-specific challenges that in-house and external legal counsel need to be aware of at each stage and explores the impact of these challenges on the transaction. This session discusses the key differences between a share purchase and an asset purchase transaction in Australia and China. It discusses some of the main advantages and disadvantages of structuring a private acquisition as a share or an asset purchase, and other issues to consider when choosing a transaction structure in Australia and China. It also outlines alternative methods for structuring a private acquisition. The session will give an overview of market conditions for private M&A in Australia and China, the implications of common deal structures and process management issues and considerations. The session will also discuss key aspects of cross-border M&A involving Australia and China, such as restrictions on foreign investment, merger control filings and national security review. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Contract formation and enforcement This session will provide a high-level overview of key requirements for a legally binding and enforceable contracts in Australia and China. The session will review key issues such as corporate authority, capacity, and other legal requirements. This session will consider matters affecting contract enforcement and legal remedies, as well as choice of law and jurisdiction issues. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Lending & taking security This session offers a high-level overview of forms of security over assets, release of security over assets, special purpose vehicles in secured lending, quasi-security, guarantees, risk areas for lenders, structuring the priority of debts, debt trading and transfer mechanisms, agent and trust concepts, enforcement of security interests, borrower insolvency and cross-border issues on loans, in each of Australia and China. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Restructuring and insolvency This session discusses, for each of Australia and China, creditors' and shareholders' ranking on a company's insolvency; mechanisms to secure unpaid debts; mandatory set-off of mutual debts on insolvency; support for distressed businesses; rescue and insolvency procedures; stakeholders' roles; liability for an insolvent company's debts; setting aside an insolvent company's pre-insolvency transactions; carrying on business during insolvency; additional finance; and multinational cases. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Resolving disputes This session gives a structured overview of the key practical issues concerning commercial dispute resolution in each of Australia and China, including court procedures; fees and funding; interim remedies; disclosure; expert evidence; appeals; class actions; enforcement; cross-border issues; and the use of ADR. In respect of ADR, this session provides a structured overview of the key practical issues concerning commercial arbitration in Australia and China, including any mandatory provisions and default rules applicable under local law, confidentiality, local courts' willingness to assist arbitration, enforcement of awards, and the available remedies, both final and interim. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04
